title: Precoding-based protocols for entanglement assisted linear computation over a quantum many-to-one network
abstract: In this work, we consider the problem of computing a linear combination over a noiseless quantum many-to-one network. There are $k$ senders, Alice$_1$, $\ldots$, Alice$_k$, and a single receiver, Bob. Each Alice$_i$ has a data vector $W_i \in \mathbb{F}^{m_i}$, where $\mathbb{F}$ is a finite field. Bob wants to compute the linear combination $Y = V_1 W_1 + V_2 W_2 + \cdots + V_k W_k \in \mathbb{F}^m$, where $V_i$ is an $m \times m_i$ matrix over $\mathbb{F}$. The senders transmit quantum states to Bob through a noiseless many-to-one quantum network, but they are not allowed to communicate with each other. The senders share entanglement among themselves, while Bob does not share this entanglement. They encode their classical information $W_i$, $i=1,\ldots,k$, into their local subsystems and transmit them to Bob so that he can recover $Y$ through a quantum measurement and subsequent post-processing. The N-Sum Box protocol proposed by Allaix et al. (2025) considers this problem under certain constraints on the linear combination and the distribution of the data vectors among the senders.   We present protocols that support the computation of a more general class of linear transformations by giving the senders access to more qudits and allowing them to judiciously precode their input symbols. The communication cost of our schemes is at most that of the best-known prior results in this area and is strictly lower in certain cases. Finally, we demonstrate that the communication cost is subadditive across instances. Specifically, we identify two linear functions for which the total cost of computing them individually is strictly larger than the cost of computing them jointly.
summary: This paper develops advanced protocols for performing linear computations over a quantum network where multiple senders share entanglement. By allowing senders to precode inputs, they overcome limitations found in previous models, enabling the computation of more general transformations. Crucially, the authors prove that jointly computing several such functions can reduce the total required communication cost below the sum of individual costs.
main_problem: The work addresses computing a general linear combination of classical data vectors ($Y = \sum V_i W_i$) over a noiseless quantum many-to-one network.
main_result: They propose protocols that support a more general class of linear transformations than previously constrained, demonstrating subadditivity in the communication cost across multiple instances.
method: The approach involves encoding classical inputs into local quantum subsystems and transmitting them through an entangled quantum channel to a single receiver for joint measurement and post-processing.
model_or_system: The model is a noiseless quantum many-to-one network where $k$ senders share entanglement, and the computation aims to reconstruct a linear combination $\mathbf{Y}$ at Bob's location.
key_observables: Communication cost (total number of transmitted qudits) and the resulting output vector $\mathbf{Y}$.
important_parameters: Number of senders ($k$), number of instances ($L$), dimensions of input/output spaces ($\mathbb{F}^{m_i}, \mathbb{F}^m$).
main_assumptions: The computation is assumed to be zero-error, and the analysis builds upon prior work concerning constraints like the Strong Self-Orthogonality (SSO) condition.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the three stages of the coding scheme: entanglement distribution, local unitary encoding/transmission by $Alice_i$, and final measurement/post-processing at Bob.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the general linear combination problem to developing protocols that relax prior constraints (like SSO), demonstrating cost improvements, and finally proving subadditivity across multiple instances.
why_interesting: While focused on abstract quantum communication complexity, the concepts of resource quantification (communication cost) and achieving super-additive benefits are fundamental theoretical tools applicable to optimizing complex quantum information processing tasks.
